content: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), defined as excessive bleeding from the genital tract following childbirth, is a leading cause of maternal death and disability, particularly in areas with limited healthcare resources. In such settings, uterotonic medications, which are commonly used to prevent and treat PPH, are often unavailable. Therefore, there is a pressing need for simple, cost-effective interventions that can be implemented in low-resource environments. Uterine massage is currently recommended as part of the routine active management of the third stage of labour, but its effectiveness in reducing postpartum blood loss remains uncertain. If proven effective, uterine massage could serve as a straightforward intervention with the potential to significantly reduce PPH and maternal mortality in under-resourced settings. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of uterine massage, performed either after childbirth or before and after the delivery of the placenta, in reducing postpartum blood loss, as well as associated morbidity and mortality. To address this, a systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register up to April 30, 2013. The review included all published, unpublished, and ongoing randomised controlled trials that compared uterine massage alone or in combination with uterotonics to no massage. Two independent researchers assessed the eligibility of the trials, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. The effects of uterine massage initiated before or after placental delivery were first analyzed separately and then combined for an overall assessment. The review included two randomised controlled trials. The first trial involved 200 women who were randomly assigned to receive either uterine massage or no massage following the delivery of the placenta. All participants underwent active management of the third stage of labour, which included the administration of oxytocin. The number of women experiencing blood loss exceeding 500 mL was small, and no statistically significant difference was observed between the groups (risk ratio [RR] 0.52, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.16 to 1.67). There were no cases of retained placenta in either group. However, the mean blood loss was significantly lower in the uterine massage group at both 30 minutes (mean difference [MD] -41.60 mL, 95% CI -75.16 to -8.04) and 60 minutes after trial entry (MD -77.40 mL, 95% CI -118.71 to -36.09). Additionally, the need for additional uterotonic medications was significantly reduced in the uterine massage group (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.50). The second trial included 1964 women from Egypt and South Africa. Participants were assigned to receive oxytocin, uterine massage, or both after the delivery of the baby but before the delivery of the placenta. The results showed no added benefit of combining uterine massage with oxytocin compared to oxytocin alone in terms of blood loss of 500 mL or more (average RR 1.56, 95% CI 0.44 to 5.49; random-effects model) or the need for additional uterotonic medications (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.85). When the results of the two trials were combined to assess the effect of uterine massage initiated either before or after placental delivery, substantial variability (heterogeneity) was observed in the outcomes related to blood loss of 500 mL or more. Using a random-effects model, no statistically significant differences were found between the groups (average RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.39 to 3.32; random-effects model). The authors concluded that the findings of this review are inconclusive and should not be used as a basis for changing current clinical practice. The included trials had limitations, and further research involving larger numbers of participants is necessary to accurately determine the effects of sustained uterine massage. It is important to note that all women in the reviewed trials received oxytocin as part of the active management of labour. Recent evidence suggests that once an oxytocic agent has been administered, the potential for further reduction in postpartum blood loss may be limited. Future trials should focus on evaluating uterine massage in settings where uterotonic medications are unavailable and should also consider women's experiences of the procedure.
